# Unit 2: Chemotherapy — general principles, sulfonamides and antibiotics

**Chemotherapy** is the treatment of infections (and cancers) with drugs that act selectively on the invading organism or abnormal cells while sparing the host. Selective toxicity is the key idea of this whole unit. Penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones are the most frequent 10-mark questions.

## 2.1 Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Antibiotic | Substance produced by a microorganism that kills or inhibits other microorganisms (penicillin from *Penicillium*, streptomycin from *Streptomyces*) |
| Antimicrobial agent (AMA) | Any natural, semisynthetic or synthetic drug that acts against microbes (includes sulfonamides, quinolones) |
| Bactericidal | Kills bacteria (penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, vancomycin) |
| Bacteriostatic | Stops multiplication; host defence clears infection (sulfonamides, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides, clindamycin) |
| Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) | Lowest concentration that prevents visible growth |
| Minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) | Lowest concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum |
| Post-antibiotic effect (PAE) | Suppression of growth that persists after the drug level falls below MIC (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) |
| Superinfection | New infection from organisms that overgrow when normal flora is suppressed by a broad-spectrum drug |

**Time- vs concentration-dependent killing**

- **Time-dependent:** effect depends on how long the level stays above MIC (β-lactams, vancomycin) → frequent dosing or infusion.
- **Concentration-dependent:** effect depends on the peak level (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) → once-daily dosing of aminoglycosides.

## 2.2 Classification of antimicrobial agents by mechanism

| Mechanism | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Inhibit cell wall synthesis | Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams, vancomycin, bacitracin, cycloserine |
| Damage cell membrane | Polymyxin B, colistin; amphotericin B and azoles (fungi) |
| Inhibit protein synthesis (30S) | Aminoglycosides, tetracyclines |
| Inhibit protein synthesis (50S) | Chloramphenicol, macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid |
| Inhibit nucleic acid synthesis/function | Fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase), rifampicin (RNA polymerase), metronidazole |
| Antimetabolites (folate pathway) | Sulfonamides, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine, dapsone |
| Inhibit viral enzymes | Acyclovir (DNA polymerase), zidovudine (reverse transcriptase), protease inhibitors |

Other classifications: by **spectrum** (narrow: penicillin G; broad: tetracyclines, chloramphenicol) and by **type of organism** (antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, antiprotozoal, anthelmintic).

## 2.3 General principles: choosing an antimicrobial

1. **Diagnosis and the likely organism** — clinical features, Gram stain, culture and sensitivity. Start **empirical** therapy in serious infections after taking samples, then switch to **definitive** therapy.
2. **Drug factors** — spectrum, bactericidal or static, tissue penetration (CSF, bone, urine, intracellular), kinetics, toxicity, cost, route.
3. **Patient factors** — age (no tetracyclines in children under 8; no fluoroquinolones in children routinely; chloramphenicol causes grey baby syndrome in neonates), pregnancy (avoid tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones; penicillins and cephalosporins are safe), renal and liver function, allergy, host defence, genetic factors (G6PD deficiency with sulfonamides).
4. **Dose and duration** adequate to eradicate infection; stop when no longer needed.
5. **Antimicrobial stewardship** — the right drug, dose and duration, to slow resistance.

### Combination of antimicrobials

**Reasons:** to prevent resistance (TB, HIV), to treat mixed infections, for synergism (penicillin + aminoglycoside in enterococcal endocarditis; sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim), for empirical treatment of serious infection, and to reduce toxicity of each drug.

**Drawbacks:** antagonism (a bacteriostatic drug can reduce the effect of a bactericidal drug that needs growing cells, such as tetracycline with penicillin), more adverse effects, superinfection, cost.

### Resistance

**Types:** natural (innate) or acquired. **Acquired** by **mutation** (vertical transfer) or by gene transfer — **conjugation** (plasmid, R factor, via sex pilus; commonest in Gram-negatives), **transduction** (bacteriophage; staphylococcal penicillinase) and **transformation** (free DNA taken up).

**Mechanisms:**

1. Drug-inactivating enzymes — β-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, chloramphenicol acetyltransferase.
2. Altered target — penicillin-binding protein 2a in MRSA, mutated DNA gyrase, methylated ribosome (macrolides).
3. Reduced permeability — loss of porins.
4. Efflux pumps — tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones.
5. Alternative metabolic pathway — sulfonamide resistance.

**Cross-resistance:** resistance to one drug carries resistance to related drugs (between tetracyclines; between macrolides and clindamycin).

### Problems of antimicrobial use

Toxicity, hypersensitivity (penicillin anaphylaxis), drug resistance, superinfection (oral thrush, *Clostridioides difficile* colitis after clindamycin or broad-spectrum drugs), masking of infection (partial treatment of syphilis or TB), and nutritional deficiency (vitamin K and B complex from loss of gut flora).

## 2.4 Sulfonamides

Sulfonamides are synthetic derivatives of sulfanilamide, structurally similar to **para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)**.

**Classification**

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Short-acting | Sulfadiazine |
| Intermediate-acting | Sulfamethoxazole |
| Long-acting | Sulfadoxine (with pyrimethamine in malaria) |
| Poorly absorbed (gut) | Sulfasalazine (ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis) |
| Topical | Silver sulfadiazine, mafenide (burns), sulfacetamide sodium (eye drops) |

**Mechanism:** bacteria must make their own folic acid. Sulfonamides **competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase**, preventing incorporation of PABA → no dihydrofolic acid → no purines and DNA → **bacteriostatic**. Humans use preformed folate, so they are spared. Pus contains PABA, so sulfonamides fail in pus; procaine (gives PABA on hydrolysis) antagonises them.

**Adverse effects:** crystalluria (keep good urine output and alkalinise), hypersensitivity (rash, fever, Stevens–Johnson syndrome), haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, kernicterus in newborns (they displace bilirubin from albumin), blood dyscrasias. Avoided in late pregnancy and neonates.

**Uses:** mainly as cotrimoxazole; sulfadiazine with pyrimethamine for toxoplasmosis; topical uses above.

## 2.5 Cotrimoxazole (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim)

**Trimethoprim** inhibits **bacterial dihydrofolate reductase** selectively (much higher affinity for the bacterial than the human enzyme). The combination produces a **sequential block** of two steps of the same pathway.

```text
 PABA + pteridine
       |  dihydropteroate synthase   <-- blocked by sulfamethoxazole
       v
 Dihydrofolic acid
       |  dihydrofolate reductase    <-- blocked by trimethoprim
       v
 Tetrahydrofolic acid --> purines, thymidine --> DNA
```

**Why combine:** synergism (the pair is bactericidal although each alone is static), lower chance of resistance, a wider spectrum. The ratio is **1 part trimethoprim : 5 parts sulfamethoxazole**, which gives an optimal **1 : 20** ratio in plasma, as the two drugs have similar half-lives.

**Uses:** urinary tract infections, respiratory infections, typhoid (resistance now common), shigellosis, *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia (drug of choice, treatment and prophylaxis in HIV), toxoplasmosis, nocardiosis.

**Adverse effects:** those of sulfonamides plus folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia), hyperkalaemia, rashes (more frequent in HIV patients).

## 2.6 β-Lactam antibiotics: penicillins

All β-lactams have a **β-lactam ring**. Penicillins have 6-aminopenicillanic acid (a thiazolidine ring fused to the β-lactam ring).

**Mechanism:** bacteria build their wall from peptidoglycan cross-linked by **transpeptidases**, which are **penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)**. β-Lactams bind PBPs and block the final **transpeptidation** step → a weak wall → autolysins act → the cell bursts in a hypotonic medium. **Bactericidal**, best on actively growing cells. Human cells have no cell wall, hence low toxicity.

```text
 NAM-NAG units + peptide side chains
        |
 transpeptidase (PBP) cross-links chains  <-- β-lactams block here
        |
 rigid peptidoglycan wall
```

**Classification**

| Group | Examples | Key point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural | Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G), procaine and benzathine penicillin (depot) | Narrow spectrum, acid-labile, penicillinase-sensitive |
| Acid-resistant | Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) | Oral |
| Penicillinase-resistant | Methicillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin | Staphylococci producing penicillinase |
| Extended spectrum: aminopenicillins | Ampicillin, amoxicillin | Also Gram-negatives (*E. coli*, *H. influenzae*) |
| Antipseudomonal | Piperacillin, carbenicillin, ticarcillin | *Pseudomonas* |
| With β-lactamase inhibitors | Amoxicillin + clavulanic acid, ampicillin + sulbactam, piperacillin + tazobactam | Inhibitor protects the penicillin |

**Penicillin G uses:** streptococcal infections (pharyngitis, rheumatic fever prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin), pneumococcal infections, meningococcal meningitis, syphilis (drug of choice), gas gangrene, tetanus, diphtheria (with antitoxin), actinomycosis, leptospirosis.

**Adverse effects:**

- **Hypersensitivity** — the main problem: rash, urticaria, fever, angioedema, and anaphylaxis (rare but fatal). Treated with adrenaline. Ask about past reactions; skin testing is used in some settings. Cross-allergy among all penicillins and partly with cephalosporins.
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction when treating syphilis (release of spirochaetal products).
- Ampicillin rash (common in infectious mononucleosis), diarrhoea.
- Very high levels: seizures; sodium or potassium overload with large IV amounts of salts.

**Probenecid** blocks tubular secretion of penicillin and prolongs its action.

### β-Lactamase inhibitors

Clavulanic acid, sulbactam and tazobactam have a β-lactam structure but little antibacterial action of their own. They bind β-lactamase irreversibly ("suicide inhibitors") and protect the partner drug.

## 2.7 Cephalosporins

Derived from *Cephalosporium acremonium*; nucleus 7-aminocephalosporanic acid. Same mechanism as penicillins; more resistant to many β-lactamases.

| Generation | Examples | Spectrum trend |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Cefazolin, cephalexin, cefadroxil | Mainly Gram-positive; surgical prophylaxis |
| Second | Cefuroxime, cefaclor, cefoxitin | Better Gram-negative, *H. influenzae*; cefoxitin covers anaerobes |
| Third | Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ceftazidime, cefoperazone, cefixime, cefpodoxime | Strong Gram-negative; ceftriaxone enters CSF; ceftazidime/cefoperazone anti-*Pseudomonas* |
| Fourth | Cefepime, cefpirome | Broad; resistant to many β-lactamases; *Pseudomonas* |
| Fifth | Ceftaroline, ceftobiprole | Active against MRSA |

**Uses:** meningitis (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime), typhoid (ceftriaxone, cefixime), gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone), hospital infections, surgical prophylaxis (cefazolin), respiratory and urinary infections.

**Adverse effects:** hypersensitivity (cross-reactivity with penicillin is low but real; avoided after penicillin anaphylaxis), pain at injection site, diarrhoea, superinfection; some with an N-methylthiotetrazole side chain (cefoperazone) cause hypoprothrombinaemia and a **disulfiram-like reaction** with alcohol; ceftriaxone may form biliary sludge.

**Other β-lactams:** **carbapenems** (imipenem with cilastatin — cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase; meropenem) have the widest spectrum and are reserved for resistant hospital infections; imipenem can cause seizures. **Monobactam:** aztreonam (Gram-negative aerobes only, no cross-allergy with penicillin).

## 2.8 Chloramphenicol

Broad-spectrum, **bacteriostatic**, originally from *Streptomyces venezuelae*.

**Mechanism:** binds the **50S** ribosomal subunit and inhibits **peptidyl transferase**, blocking peptide bond formation.

**Kinetics:** well absorbed orally, enters CSF and the eye well; inactivated in the liver by **glucuronidation**; an enzyme inhibitor.

**Adverse effects:**

1. **Bone marrow depression** — (a) dose-related, reversible suppression of red cell maturation; (b) idiosyncratic, irreversible **aplastic anaemia**, not related to dose, often fatal. This is why use is restricted.
2. **Grey baby syndrome** — newborns lack glucuronyl transferase and have poor renal excretion; the drug accumulates → vomiting, cyanosis (ashen grey colour), hypothermia, circulatory collapse.
3. Hypersensitivity, superinfection, optic neuritis.
4. Interactions: inhibits metabolism of phenytoin, warfarin and tolbutamide.

**Uses (restricted):** bacterial meningitis and brain abscess when safer drugs cannot be used, typhoid (where sensitive), rickettsial infections, anaerobic infections, and topically in eye infections.

## 2.9 Macrolides

Erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin, roxithromycin (large lactone ring).

**Mechanism:** bind the **50S** subunit (23S rRNA) and block **translocation** of the growing peptide chain. Bacteriostatic (bactericidal at high levels). Resistance by efflux or ribosomal methylation (*erm* genes).

**Uses:** atypical pneumonia (*Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia*, *Legionella*), whooping cough, diphtheria carriers, streptococcal infection in penicillin-allergic patients, *H. pylori* (clarithromycin), *Mycobacterium avium* complex (clarithromycin, azithromycin), chlamydial urethritis (single-dose azithromycin), trachoma, typhoid (azithromycin).

**Adverse effects:** gastric upset (erythromycin is a **motilin agonist**), cholestatic hepatitis (erythromycin estolate), QT prolongation, ototoxicity at high levels.

**Interactions:** erythromycin and clarithromycin **inhibit CYP3A4** → raise levels of theophylline, carbamazepine, warfarin, statins and some antihistamines (arrhythmias). Azithromycin inhibits the enzyme least.

**Azithromycin advantages:** acid-stable, high tissue and intracellular levels, very long half-life (once-daily, short courses), fewer interactions.

## 2.10 Quinolones and fluoroquinolones

**Nalidixic acid** is the first-generation quinolone (urinary antiseptic, mostly Gram-negative). Adding fluorine gave **fluoroquinolones (FQs)**.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| First generation FQs | Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin |
| Respiratory FQs (newer) | Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gemifloxacin |

**Mechanism:** inhibit **DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II)** — the main target in Gram-negatives — and **topoisomerase IV** — the main target in Gram-positives. Gyrase introduces negative supercoils needed for DNA replication; blocking it causes DNA breaks → **bactericidal**, concentration-dependent killing with a post-antibiotic effect.

**Uses:** urinary tract infections, gonorrhoea (resistance now high), typhoid (resistance common), bacterial diarrhoea, bone and joint infections, respiratory infections (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), multidrug-resistant TB (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), anthrax, prophylaxis in neutropenia.

**Adverse effects:** GI upset, CNS effects (dizziness, headache, seizures in predisposed patients), **tendinitis and tendon rupture** (Achilles tendon, more in the elderly and with steroids), damage to growing cartilage (avoided in children and pregnancy except when necessary), photosensitivity, QT prolongation (moxifloxacin), dysglycaemia, peripheral neuropathy.

**Interactions:** absorption reduced by antacids, iron, calcium and zinc (chelation); ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 → theophylline toxicity; with NSAIDs, a higher risk of seizures.

## 2.11 Tetracyclines

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Older | Tetracycline, oxytetracycline |
| Newer, long-acting | Doxycycline, minocycline |
| Glycylcycline | Tigecycline |

**Mechanism:** actively taken into bacteria; bind the **30S** subunit and prevent attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the acceptor (A) site → protein synthesis stops. Broad-spectrum, **bacteriostatic**. Resistance mainly by efflux pumps and ribosomal protection proteins.

**Kinetics:** form insoluble chelates with Ca2+, Mg2+, Al3+ and Fe2+ (milk, antacids, iron reduce absorption, except doxycycline is affected less); deposit in growing bones and teeth. Doxycycline is excreted mainly in faeces, so it is the tetracycline safe in renal failure.

**Uses:** rickettsial infections (typhus, scrub typhus — doxycycline is the drug of choice), *Mycoplasma* and *Chlamydia* infections, cholera, brucellosis (with streptomycin or rifampicin), plague, leptospirosis prophylaxis, acne (doxycycline, minocycline), malaria prophylaxis and treatment (doxycycline), *H. pylori* (quadruple therapy), Lyme disease.

**Adverse effects:**

- GI irritation; oesophageal ulcers (take with plenty of water, sitting up).
- **Teeth and bones:** brown discolouration and enamel hypoplasia of teeth; reduced bone growth → avoided in pregnancy, lactation and children under 8.
- Superinfection (candidiasis, *C. difficile*).
- Phototoxicity (demeclocycline, doxycycline).
- Hepatotoxicity (high doses, pregnancy); renal: expired (degraded) tetracycline causes Fanconi syndrome; worsens renal failure (except doxycycline).
- Vestibular toxicity (minocycline); raised intracranial pressure in infants.

## 2.12 Aminoglycosides

Streptomycin, gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, kanamycin, neomycin, netilmicin, sisomicin.

**Mechanism:** enter bacteria by an **oxygen-dependent** transport, so they are inactive against anaerobes. They bind the **30S** subunit → (1) block the initiation complex, (2) **misreading of mRNA** producing faulty proteins that insert into the membrane and increase permeability, (3) break up polysomes → **bactericidal**, concentration-dependent with a post-antibiotic effect. β-Lactams help their entry → synergy.

**Common properties**

1. Highly polar, **not absorbed orally** (neomycin used orally for gut action); given IM or IV.
2. Do not enter CSF or cells well; excreted unchanged by the kidney.
3. Narrow therapeutic index; levels monitored.
4. Active mainly against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli; streptomycin and amikacin against *M. tuberculosis*.
5. Less effective in acidic and anaerobic sites (pus, abscess).

**Adverse effects**

| Toxicity | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Ototoxicity | Damage to hair cells: vestibular (streptomycin, gentamicin) or cochlear (amikacin, neomycin, kanamycin); may be permanent; worse with loop diuretics |
| Nephrotoxicity | Proximal tubular damage; usually reversible; worse with vancomycin, amphotericin B, cephalosporins, NSAIDs |
| Neuromuscular blockade | Reduce acetylcholine release (calcium antagonism) → respiratory paralysis risk with neuromuscular blockers, in myasthenia gravis; reversed by calcium |
| Others | Hypersensitivity (streptomycin) |

Avoided in pregnancy (fetal ear damage). **Once-daily dosing** gives a high peak (better killing, longer PAE) with lower trough levels (less toxicity).

**Uses:** gentamicin/amikacin for serious Gram-negative infections (septicaemia, hospital infections, often with a β-lactam), with penicillin in enterococcal and streptococcal endocarditis; streptomycin in TB, plague and tularaemia; amikacin in MDR-TB; neomycin topically and orally for bowel preparation and hepatic encephalopathy; tobramycin in *Pseudomonas* infections (inhaled in cystic fibrosis).

## Remember

- Selective toxicity; bactericidal (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, FQs) vs bacteriostatic (sulfonamides, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides).
- Resistance: mutation, conjugation (R plasmid), transduction, transformation; mechanisms: enzymes, altered target, permeability, efflux.
- Sulfonamide: PABA analogue, inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits bacterial DHFR; cotrimoxazole = sequential block, 1:5 tablet → 1:20 plasma; drug of choice in *Pneumocystis* pneumonia.
- Penicillins block transpeptidase (PBP); anaphylaxis → adrenaline; benzathine penicillin for rheumatic fever prophylaxis; drug of choice for syphilis.
- Clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam: suicide β-lactamase inhibitors.
- Cephalosporin generations: 3rd ceftriaxone (meningitis, typhoid, gonorrhoea); 5th ceftaroline (MRSA); disulfiram-like reaction with cefoperazone.
- Chloramphenicol: 50S, peptidyl transferase; aplastic anaemia, grey baby syndrome.
- Macrolides: 50S translocation; erythromycin a CYP3A4 inhibitor and motilin agonist; azithromycin long half-life.
- FQs: DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV; tendon rupture, cartilage damage, QT; chelate with antacids.
- Tetracyclines: 30S A-site; teeth/bone staining; doxycycline drug of choice in rickettsial infections, safe in renal failure.
- Aminoglycosides: 30S misreading, oxygen-dependent entry; ototoxic, nephrotoxic, neuromuscular block; once-daily dosing.

# Unit 3: Chemotherapy of tuberculosis, leprosy, fungal, viral, worm, malarial and amoebic infections

This unit continues chemotherapy with seven groups of drugs. Each group is examined the same way: classification, mechanism, uses, adverse effects. First-line antitubercular drugs, antimalarials and antiretroviral drugs are the favourite 10-mark questions; amphotericin B, dapsone, metronidazole and albendazole are favourite short notes.

## 3.1 Antitubercular drugs

**Tuberculosis** is caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, a slow-growing, acid-fast bacillus with a waxy, lipid-rich wall (mycolic acid). It lives inside macrophages and in caseous lesions, and some bacilli stay dormant for long periods. So TB needs **several drugs together for months**.

**Why multidrug therapy?**

1. To prevent drug resistance (any large bacillary population contains naturally resistant mutants).
2. To kill different populations: rapidly multiplying extracellular bacilli (isoniazid), slowly multiplying intracellular bacilli in acidic macrophages (pyrazinamide), and intermittently active bacilli in caseous material (rifampicin).
3. To shorten the total duration of treatment.

### Classification

| Line | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| First-line (HRZE + S) | Isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), ethambutol (E), streptomycin (S) |
| Second-line: fluoroquinolones | Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin |
| Second-line: injectables | Amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin |
| Other second-line | Ethionamide, cycloserine, para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), linezolid, clofazimine |
| Newer drugs | Bedaquiline, delamanid, pretomanid |

### First-line drugs

| Drug | Mechanism | Action | Key adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Isoniazid | Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG); inhibits **mycolic acid** synthesis | Bactericidal on rapidly dividing bacilli; most potent | **Peripheral neuropathy** (pyridoxine deficiency; prevented by pyridoxine), **hepatitis** (more in elderly and alcoholics), CNS effects; slow acetylators have higher levels |
| Rifampicin | Inhibits DNA-dependent **RNA polymerase** | Bactericidal on all populations, including intermittently active bacilli | Hepatitis, **orange-red urine, tears, sweat** (stains contact lenses), flu-like syndrome on intermittent use, thrombocytopenia; a potent **enzyme inducer** |
| Pyrazinamide | Converted to pyrazinoic acid; works in **acidic pH** inside macrophages | Bactericidal on intracellular bacilli; sterilising in first 2 months | **Hepatotoxicity**, **hyperuricaemia** (gout), arthralgia |
| Ethambutol | Inhibits **arabinosyl transferase** (arabinogalactan of the wall) | Bacteriostatic; prevents resistance | **Optic neuritis** (reduced visual acuity and red–green colour vision); avoided in young children who cannot report vision changes |
| Streptomycin | 30S ribosome (aminoglycoside) | Bactericidal on extracellular bacilli | Ototoxicity (vestibular), nephrotoxicity; now rarely used |

**Rifampicin interactions:** by inducing CYP3A4 it lowers levels of oral contraceptives (failure), warfarin, corticosteroids, oral antidiabetics, protease inhibitors and many others. **Isoniazid** inhibits metabolism of phenytoin and carbamazepine.

### Treatment regimens (National TB Elimination Programme, India)

TB treatment has an **intensive phase** (four drugs: H, R, Z, E for 2 months) followed by a **continuation phase** (H, R, E for 4 months) for drug-sensitive TB, given as daily **fixed-dose combinations** by weight band. The programme follows the principle of **directly observed treatment** (DOTS) with patient support.

**Drug-resistant TB:**

- **MDR-TB:** resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin.
- **Pre-XDR-TB:** MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to a fluoroquinolone.
- **XDR-TB:** pre-XDR plus resistance to bedaquiline and/or linezolid (current WHO definition).

Treated with all-oral regimens based on bedaquiline, linezolid, fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), clofazimine, cycloserine, and pretomanid-based regimens, as per programme guidelines. Bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial **ATP synthase**; it prolongs the QT interval.

**Chemoprophylaxis (TB preventive therapy):** isoniazid alone, or isoniazid with rifapentine, in close contacts and people living with HIV, as per guidelines.

## 3.2 Antileprotic drugs

**Leprosy** (Hansen's disease) is caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*, which affects skin and peripheral nerves. Clinically classified as **paucibacillary** (PB; up to 5 skin lesions) and **multibacillary** (MB; more than 5 lesions, or nerve involvement, or smear positive).

| Drug | Mechanism | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dapsone (diaminodiphenyl sulfone) | PABA antagonist; inhibits folate synthesis (like sulfonamides) | Bacteriostatic; haemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency), methaemoglobinaemia, "dapsone syndrome" (rash, fever, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy) |
| Rifampicin | RNA polymerase | Rapidly bactericidal; given once monthly in MDT |
| Clofazimine | Binds mycobacterial DNA; also anti-inflammatory | **Reddish-black skin pigmentation**, dry skin, GI upset; useful in type 2 lepra reaction |
| Others | Ofloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin | Alternative regimens |

**Multidrug therapy (MDT, WHO):** rifampicin (monthly, supervised) + clofazimine (monthly supervised plus daily) + dapsone (daily). WHO now recommends the **same three-drug regimen for both PB and MB** leprosy, differing in duration (6 months for PB, 12 months for MB).

**Lepra reactions:**

- **Type 1 (reversal reaction):** a cell-mediated immune flare in existing lesions and nerves → corticosteroids (prednisolone).
- **Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL):** an immune-complex reaction with painful nodules and fever → corticosteroids, clofazimine, thalidomide (strictly avoided in pregnancy because it causes phocomelia).

## 3.3 Antifungal agents

Fungal cell membranes contain **ergosterol** instead of cholesterol — the main target of selective toxicity.

| Class | Examples | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polyene antibiotics | Amphotericin B, nystatin, natamycin | Bind ergosterol → form **pores** in the membrane → leakage of ions → fungal death |
| Echinocandins | Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin | Inhibit **β-(1,3)-glucan synthase** → defective cell wall |
| Azoles: imidazoles | Ketoconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole | Inhibit fungal CYP450 enzyme **lanosterol 14α-demethylase** → no ergosterol |
| Azoles: triazoles | Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole | Same, more selective for fungal enzyme |
| Allylamine | Terbinafine | Inhibits **squalene epoxidase** (ergosterol synthesis) |
| Antimetabolite | Flucytosine | Converted to 5-fluorouracil in fungal cells → inhibits DNA synthesis |
| Others | Griseofulvin | Binds tubulin, inhibits fungal mitosis; deposits in keratin |
| Topical | Ciclopirox, tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), amorolfine | Superficial infections |

### Amphotericin B

Broad-spectrum, fungicidal; the drug of choice for many serious systemic fungal infections (cryptococcal meningitis with flucytosine, invasive aspergillosis in some settings, mucormycosis, histoplasmosis); also used in **kala-azar** (visceral leishmaniasis). Given IV, as it is not absorbed orally.

**Adverse effects:** infusion reactions (fever, chills, rigors, headache, hypotension) — reduced by premedication and slow infusion; **nephrotoxicity** (the main dose-limiting effect), hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, anaemia, thrombophlebitis. **Lipid formulations** (liposomal amphotericin B) are less nephrotoxic.

### Azoles

- **Ketoconazole:** first oral azole; inhibits human CYP enzymes too → blocks steroid synthesis (gynaecomastia, menstrual changes) and causes interactions; hepatotoxic; now mostly topical. Systemic use is used in Cushing's syndrome in selected cases.
- **Fluconazole:** water-soluble, good oral absorption, enters CSF; used in candidiasis (vaginal, oral, oesophageal), cryptococcal meningitis (maintenance), prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients. Fewer interactions.
- **Itraconazole:** aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, onychomycosis; absorption needs acid and food.
- **Voriconazole:** drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis; visual disturbances.
- **Posaconazole, isavuconazole:** also active against mucormycosis.
- Azoles inhibit CYP3A4 → raise levels of warfarin, statins, cyclosporine.

**Griseofulvin** is fungistatic, given orally for dermatophyte infections of skin, hair and nails (not active topically or against *Candida*); an enzyme inducer, teratogenic. **Terbinafine** is fungicidal and preferred for onychomycosis. **Nystatin** is too toxic for injection; used for oral and vaginal candidiasis.

## 3.4 Antiviral drugs

Viruses use host cell machinery, so selective targets are viral enzymes or steps of the replication cycle (attachment, entry, uncoating, nucleic acid synthesis, assembly, release).

| Group | Examples | Mechanism / use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anti-herpes | Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir, ganciclovir (CMV), foscarnet | Inhibit viral DNA polymerase |
| Anti-influenza | Oseltamivir, zanamivir; amantadine, rimantadine (older) | Neuraminidase inhibitors block release of new virions; amantadine blocks M2 ion channel (uncoating) |
| Anti-hepatitis B | Tenofovir, entecavir, lamivudine, interferon-α | Polymerase (reverse transcriptase) inhibition; immune activity |
| Anti-hepatitis C | Sofosbuvir, daclatasvir, velpatasvir, ledipasvir | NS5B polymerase and NS5A inhibitors (direct-acting antivirals) |
| Anti-HIV (antiretroviral) | See below | |
| Others | Ribavirin, remdesivir, molnupiravir | RNA viruses |

### Acyclovir

A guanosine analogue. **Viral thymidine kinase** phosphorylates it to the monophosphate (so it is activated only in infected cells — the basis of selectivity); host kinases make acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and causes **chain termination**. Used in herpes simplex (genital, labial, keratitis, encephalitis — drug of choice) and varicella-zoster. Adverse effects: renal crystal formation on rapid IV infusion, CNS effects. **Valacyclovir** is a prodrug with better oral bioavailability. **Ganciclovir** (CMV) causes bone marrow suppression.

### Antiretroviral drugs (HIV)

HIV is an RNA retrovirus that infects CD4 T cells.

```text
 HIV life cycle and drug targets
 attachment to CD4 + CCR5/CXCR4  <-- maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist)
 fusion                           <-- enfuvirtide
 reverse transcription RNA->DNA   <-- NRTIs, NNRTIs
 integration into host DNA        <-- integrase inhibitors
 protein processing (protease)    <-- protease inhibitors
 budding and maturation
```

| Class | Examples | Key adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NRTIs (nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors) | Zidovudine, lamivudine, emtricitabine, abacavir, tenofovir | Zidovudine: bone marrow suppression (anaemia); abacavir: hypersensitivity; tenofovir: renal toxicity, bone loss; class: lactic acidosis |
| NNRTIs | Efavirenz, nevirapine, rilpivirine, etravirine | Efavirenz: CNS effects, vivid dreams; nevirapine: rash, hepatotoxicity |
| Protease inhibitors (PIs) | Lopinavir, ritonavir, atazanavir, darunavir | Lipodystrophy, hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia; ritonavir is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor used to "boost" other PIs |
| Integrase inhibitors (INSTIs) | Dolutegravir, raltegravir, bictegravir | Generally well tolerated; weight gain |
| Entry/fusion inhibitors | Maraviroc, enfuvirtide | |

NRTIs are phosphorylated by host kinases; as nucleotide analogues lacking a 3′-OH group, they cause **chain termination**. NNRTIs bind a non-catalytic site of reverse transcriptase (non-competitive).

**Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART / ART):** a combination of three drugs, usually two NRTIs plus one drug from another class. The preferred first-line regimen in India (National AIDS Control Programme) is **tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD)**. Combination prevents resistance and keeps viral load suppressed. ART is also used for prevention of mother-to-child transmission and for post-exposure prophylaxis.

## 3.5 Anthelmintics

Drugs that kill or expel parasitic worms (helminths): nematodes (roundworms), cestodes (tapeworms) and trematodes (flukes).

| Drug | Mechanism | Main uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Albendazole, mebendazole (benzimidazoles) | Bind β-tubulin → block microtubule formation → impaired glucose uptake, worm dies slowly | Broad: roundworm, hookworm, whipworm, pinworm; albendazole for neurocysticercosis and hydatid disease |
| Pyrantel pamoate | Depolarising neuromuscular blocker in worms → **spastic paralysis** | Roundworm, hookworm, pinworm |
| Piperazine | GABA agonist at worm muscle → **flaccid paralysis** | Roundworm, pinworm (older) |
| Ivermectin | Opens glutamate-gated Cl− channels → hyperpolarisation, paralysis | Onchocerciasis (drug of choice), strongyloidiasis, scabies, head lice, filariasis (mass drug administration) |
| Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) | Makes microfilariae susceptible to host immunity | Lymphatic filariasis; tropical eosinophilia |
| Praziquantel | Increases Ca2+ permeability → contraction and paralysis, tegument damage | Schistosomiasis, tapeworms, flukes, neurocysticercosis |
| Niclosamide | Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in tapeworm | Tapeworms (not effective against larval cysts) |
| Levamisole | Nicotinic agonist → spastic paralysis; also immunostimulant | Roundworm |

**Mazzotti reaction** — itching, fever and rash from dying microfilariae after DEC (in onchocerciasis especially). Pyrantel and piperazine are antagonists and should not be combined. India runs national **deworming** campaigns with albendazole for school children and mass drug administration for filariasis (DEC + albendazole, with ivermectin in some areas).

## 3.6 Antimalarial drugs

Malaria is caused by *Plasmodium falciparum*, *P. vivax*, *P. ovale*, *P. malariae* and *P. knowlesi*, spread by the female *Anopheles* mosquito.

```text
 Malarial life cycle and drug actions

 Sporozoites (mosquito bite)
        |
 Liver (pre-erythrocytic) ......... primaquine, proguanil (causal prophylaxis)
        |        \
        |         hypnozoites (vivax, ovale) -- relapse --> primaquine, tafenoquine
        v
 Red cell (erythrocytic schizogony) - fever .. chloroquine, artemisinins,
        |                                      quinine, mefloquine (schizonticides)
        v
 Gametocytes (taken up by mosquito) .... primaquine (gametocidal, falciparum)
```

**Classification by stage of action**

| Class | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Erythrocytic (blood) schizonticides | Chloroquine, quinine, mefloquine, artemisinins (artesunate, artemether, arteether), lumefantrine, amodiaquine, piperaquine, atovaquone, proguanil, pyrimethamine, doxycycline |
| Tissue schizonticides (causal prophylaxis) | Primaquine, proguanil |
| Hypnozoiticides (radical cure, anti-relapse) | Primaquine, tafenoquine |
| Gametocides | Primaquine (falciparum); chloroquine and quinine (vivax) |

**By chemical class:** 4-aminoquinolines (chloroquine, amodiaquine), quinoline methanol (mefloquine), cinchona alkaloids (quinine), 8-aminoquinolines (primaquine, tafenoquine), biguanides (proguanil), diaminopyrimidines (pyrimethamine), artemisinin derivatives, amino alcohols (lumefantrine), naphthoquinone (atovaquone), antibiotics (doxycycline, clindamycin).

### Chloroquine

**Mechanism:** a weak base that concentrates in the acidic food vacuole of the parasite. The parasite digests haemoglobin and converts toxic free haem into harmless **haemozoin** by polymerisation. Chloroquine **inhibits haem polymerase**, so free haem accumulates and kills the parasite.

**Uses:** treatment of *P. vivax* malaria (with primaquine for radical cure), extraintestinal amoebiasis (liver abscess), rheumatoid arthritis and lupus (hydroxychloroquine), discoid lupus. *P. falciparum* is widely resistant.

**Adverse effects:** nausea, itching (especially in people of African descent), headache, visual disturbances; long-term use causes **retinopathy** (bull's-eye maculopathy) and corneal deposits; QT prolongation; worsens psoriasis.

### Artemisinin derivatives and ACT

Artesunate, artemether and arteether come from *Artemisia annua* (qinghaosu). They contain an **endoperoxide bridge** that is activated by haem iron to form free radicals that damage parasite proteins. They act fast and also reduce gametocytes. Because of their short half-life and to prevent resistance, they are always given as **artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)** with a longer-acting partner:

- Artesunate + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (used in India's programme for uncomplicated falciparum malaria, except in the north-eastern states).
- Artemether + lumefantrine (north-eastern states, where SP resistance is common).
- Others: artesunate + mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine.

**Severe malaria:** injectable **artesunate** is the drug of choice (quinine as an alternative); then a full course of ACT.

### Quinine

From cinchona bark. Blood schizonticide (haem polymerase inhibition). Used in severe falciparum malaria when artesunate is not available, and in the first trimester of pregnancy in some guidelines. Adverse effects: **cinchonism** (tinnitus, deafness, headache, nausea, blurred vision), **hypoglycaemia** (it releases insulin), arrhythmias, haemolysis (blackwater fever), uterine stimulation.

### Primaquine

An 8-aminoquinoline that forms oxidant metabolites damaging parasite mitochondria. Kills liver hypnozoites → **radical cure of vivax and ovale malaria**; a single low dose kills falciparum gametocytes and blocks transmission. **Haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency** — test for G6PD before radical cure. Avoided in pregnancy and in infants. **Tafenoquine** is a single-dose long-acting relative.

### Other antimalarials

- **Mefloquine:** prophylaxis and treatment of resistant falciparum; neuropsychiatric effects.
- **Proguanil:** a biguanide converted to cycloguanil, which inhibits plasmodial DHFR; used with atovaquone (Malarone) for prophylaxis.
- **Pyrimethamine** with sulfadoxine: sequential folate block (like cotrimoxazole).
- **Doxycycline:** prophylaxis for travellers; with quinine in treatment.

**Chemoprophylaxis** for travellers to areas of chloroquine-resistant malaria: doxycycline, mefloquine or atovaquone–proguanil, started before travel and continued afterwards.

## 3.7 Antiamoebic drugs

**Amoebiasis** is caused by *Entamoeba histolytica*: intestinal (dysentery, colitis), extraintestinal (amoebic liver abscess) and asymptomatic cyst passers.

| Class | Examples | Site of action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tissue amoebicides (intestinal wall + liver) | Nitroimidazoles: metronidazole, tinidazole, secnidazole, ornidazole | Both intestinal and extraintestinal |
| Tissue amoebicides (liver only) | Chloroquine | Liver abscess |
| Tissue amoebicides (older) | Emetine, dehydroemetine | Toxic; rarely used |
| Luminal amoebicides | Diloxanide furoate, iodoquinol (diiodohydroxyquinoline), paromomycin, tetracyclines (indirect) | Cysts and trophozoites in the gut lumen |

### Metronidazole

**Mechanism:** a prodrug. In anaerobic organisms its nitro group is **reduced** (by ferredoxin-linked enzymes) to reactive intermediates that damage DNA → cidal. Human cells and aerobes lack this reducing system — selective toxicity.

**Spectrum and uses:** amoebiasis (intestinal and liver abscess — drug of choice), giardiasis, trichomoniasis (drug of choice; treat the partner too), anaerobic infections (*Bacteroides fragilis*, *Clostridia*), *C. difficile* colitis (now vancomycin or fidaxomicin preferred in many guidelines), *H. pylori* (part of regimens), bacterial vaginosis, dental infections, prophylaxis in colorectal surgery.

**Adverse effects:** metallic taste, nausea, dark urine, headache, peripheral neuropathy and seizures with long use; a **disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol** (alcohol is avoided during treatment and for some time after); enhances warfarin effect.

After a tissue amoebicide, a **luminal amoebicide** (diloxanide furoate) is given to eradicate cysts and prevent relapse.

## Remember

- TB: multidrug therapy prevents resistance and kills all bacillary populations; intensive phase HRZE for 2 months + continuation HRE.
- Isoniazid → neuropathy (give pyridoxine), hepatitis; rifampicin → orange urine, enzyme inducer, contraceptive failure; pyrazinamide → hyperuricaemia; ethambutol → optic neuritis.
- MDR-TB = resistant to H and R; bedaquiline inhibits ATP synthase.
- Leprosy MDT: rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone; clofazimine pigmentation; dapsone haemolysis; ENL → steroids, thalidomide.
- Antifungals: polyenes form pores in ergosterol membrane; azoles inhibit 14α-demethylase; terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase; echinocandins inhibit glucan synthase; amphotericin B is nephrotoxic.
- Acyclovir needs viral thymidine kinase; oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase; ART = three drugs, TLD first line in India; ritonavir boosts PIs.
- Benzimidazoles bind β-tubulin; pyrantel spastic, piperazine flaccid paralysis; ivermectin for onchocerciasis and scabies; praziquantel for flukes and tapeworms.
- Chloroquine inhibits haem polymerase; ACT for falciparum; IV artesunate for severe malaria; primaquine for radical cure, check G6PD; quinine causes cinchonism and hypoglycaemia.
- Metronidazole: reduced in anaerobes; drug of choice for amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; follow with diloxanide furoate.

# Unit 4: UTI and STD, cancer chemotherapy and immunopharmacology

This unit closes chemotherapy with drugs for urinary tract infections, sexually transmitted diseases and cancer, and then turns to drugs that boost or suppress the immune system, including biological drugs such as monoclonal antibodies and biosimilars. Classification of anticancer drugs and immunosuppressants are the classic long questions.

## 4.1 Urinary tract infections (UTI)

**UTI** is infection anywhere in the urinary tract: lower (cystitis, urethritis) or upper (pyelonephritis). The commonest organism is ***Escherichia coli***; others are *Klebsiella*, *Proteus*, *Enterococcus*, *Staphylococcus saprophyticus* and, in hospital and catheter infections, *Pseudomonas*. Women get UTI more often because of the short urethra.

### Drugs for UTI

| Group | Examples | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Urinary antiseptics | Nitrofurantoin, methenamine (hexamine) mandelate, nalidixic acid | Act only in urine; no systemic antibacterial levels |
| Fosfomycin | Fosfomycin trometamol | Single-dose oral for uncomplicated cystitis; inhibits an early step of cell wall synthesis (MurA) |
| Cotrimoxazole, trimethoprim | | Cystitis where local resistance is low; prophylaxis of recurrent UTI |
| Fluoroquinolones | Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin | Complicated UTI, pyelonephritis; avoid for simple cystitis to spare them |
| β-Lactams | Amoxicillin–clavulanate, cephalexin, cefixime, ceftriaxone; carbapenems for resistant organisms | Safe in pregnancy |
| Aminoglycosides | Gentamicin, amikacin | Severe pyelonephritis, hospital UTI |

**Nitrofurantoin:** reduced by bacterial flavoproteins to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and ribosomes; reaches effective levels only in urine, so used for lower UTI (not pyelonephritis). Adverse effects: nausea, brown urine, peripheral neuropathy, pulmonary reactions (acute pneumonitis; fibrosis on long use), haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Not used when kidney function is poor (fails to reach urine and toxicity rises).

**Methenamine:** in **acidic urine** it releases **formaldehyde**, which is antibacterial. Urine must be acidic (pH below about 5.5), so it is given with an acidifier; ineffective with urea-splitting *Proteus* (alkaline urine). Used only for prophylaxis.

**Urinary analgesic:** phenazopyridine relieves burning (colours urine orange-red); it has no antibacterial action.

**General measures:** plenty of fluids, frequent voiding, treat obstruction or stones, remove catheters when possible. **Asymptomatic bacteriuria** is treated in pregnancy (risk of pyelonephritis and preterm birth) but usually not in others.

## 4.2 Sexually transmitted diseases (STD)

The National AIDS and STI Control Programme in India uses a **syndromic approach**: treat all likely causes of a syndrome (urethral discharge, genital ulcer, vaginal discharge) at the first visit, because laboratory diagnosis may not be available and patients may not return. Colour-coded STI kits are used.

| Disease (organism) | Treatment of choice (drug classes) |
| --- | --- |
| Syphilis (*Treponema pallidum*) | **Benzathine penicillin G**; doxycycline in penicillin allergy (not in pregnancy) |
| Gonorrhoea (*Neisseria gonorrhoeae*) | **Ceftriaxone** (with azithromycin or doxycycline for possible chlamydial co-infection) |
| Chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis, lymphogranuloma venereum | Azithromycin or doxycycline |
| Chancroid (*Haemophilus ducreyi*) | Azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin |
| Donovanosis (*Klebsiella granulomatis*) | Azithromycin, doxycycline |
| Trichomoniasis | Metronidazole or tinidazole (treat partner) |
| Bacterial vaginosis | Metronidazole, clindamycin |
| Vulvovaginal candidiasis | Clotrimazole (topical), fluconazole (oral) |
| Genital herpes | Acyclovir, valacyclovir |
| Genital warts (HPV) | Podophyllotoxin, imiquimod; prevented by HPV vaccine |
| HIV | Antiretroviral therapy (Unit 3) |

Principles: treat sexual partners, counsel on condom use, test for HIV and syphilis, follow up.

## 4.3 Cancer chemotherapy: principles

Cancer cells divide without control. Most anticancer drugs act on **dividing cells**, so they also damage normal fast-dividing tissues: bone marrow, gut lining, hair follicles, gonads and the fetus.

### Cell cycle and drug specificity

```text
            G1 (growth)  -->  S (DNA synthesis)
            ^                        |
            |                        v
     M (mitosis)  <------------  G2 (preparation)
            |
            v
     G0 (resting cells, insensitive to most drugs)

 S phase:  antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-FU, cytarabine, 6-MP)
 G2 phase: bleomycin, etoposide, topotecan
 M phase:  vinca alkaloids, taxanes
 Cell-cycle non-specific: alkylating agents, platinum, anthracyclines
```

- **Cell-cycle specific (CCS)** drugs act in a particular phase; effective on tumours with a high growth fraction (leukaemias, lymphomas).
- **Cell-cycle non-specific (CCNS)** drugs kill both cycling and resting cells; useful in solid tumours with a low growth fraction.

### Log-kill hypothesis

Each course kills a **constant fraction** (not a constant number) of tumour cells. A course that kills 99.9% (3-log kill) reduces 10^12 cells to 10^9. So repeated courses are needed, and treatment continues after the tumour is no longer detectable.

### Principles of use

1. **Combination chemotherapy** — drugs with different mechanisms and non-overlapping toxicities, each active alone (e.g. CHOP for lymphoma, ABVD for Hodgkin's lymphoma). It raises cell kill and delays resistance.
2. **Intermittent courses (cycles)** allow the bone marrow and gut to recover between courses.
3. **Adjuvant** chemotherapy after surgery or radiation removes micrometastases; **neoadjuvant** chemotherapy shrinks a tumour before surgery.
4. **Supportive care:** anti-emetics (ondansetron, aprepitant, dexamethasone), growth factors (filgrastim for neutropenia), allopurinol or rasburicase for **tumour lysis syndrome** (hyperuricaemia), mesna with cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide, folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue after high-dose methotrexate.

### Common toxicities

Bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, infection, bleeding), nausea and vomiting, mucositis and diarrhoea, alopecia, sterility, teratogenicity, hyperuricaemia, delayed wound healing, and secondary cancers (alkylating agents).

**Drug-specific toxicities** (frequently asked): cyclophosphamide — haemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein; prevented by mesna); cisplatin — nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, severe vomiting; doxorubicin — cardiotoxicity; bleomycin — pulmonary fibrosis; vincristine — peripheral neuropathy; methotrexate — mucositis, hepatotoxicity; busulfan — pulmonary fibrosis, hyperpigmentation; L-asparaginase — pancreatitis, hypersensitivity.

## 4.4 Classification of anticancer drugs

| Class | Sub-class | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Cytotoxic drugs | | |
| 1. Alkylating agents | Nitrogen mustards | Cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, chlorambucil, melphalan, mechlorethamine |
| | Nitrosoureas | Carmustine, lomustine (enter the brain) |
| | Alkyl sulfonate | Busulfan |
| | Triazenes | Dacarbazine, temozolomide |
| | Platinum compounds | Cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin |
| 2. Antimetabolites | Folate antagonist | Methotrexate, pemetrexed |
| | Purine antagonists | 6-Mercaptopurine, 6-thioguanine, fludarabine |
| | Pyrimidine antagonists | 5-Fluorouracil, capecitabine, cytarabine, gemcitabine |
| 3. Natural products | Vinca alkaloids | Vincristine, vinblastine |
| | Taxanes | Paclitaxel, docetaxel |
| | Epipodophyllotoxins | Etoposide |
| | Camptothecins | Topotecan, irinotecan |
| | Antitumour antibiotics | Doxorubicin, daunorubicin, bleomycin, actinomycin D, mitomycin C |
| | Enzyme | L-Asparaginase |
| 4. Miscellaneous | | Hydroxyurea, imatinib-type agents (see targeted drugs) |
| B. Hormonal drugs | Glucocorticoids | Prednisolone (leukaemias, lymphomas) |
| | Anti-oestrogens / SERMs | Tamoxifen, fulvestrant |
| | Aromatase inhibitors | Letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane |
| | Anti-androgens | Flutamide, bicalutamide, enzalutamide; abiraterone (inhibits androgen synthesis) |
| | GnRH analogues | Leuprolide, goserelin |
| | Progestins | Medroxyprogesterone (endometrial cancer) |
| C. Targeted drugs | Kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies | See section 4.8 |

### Mechanisms of the main groups

- **Alkylating agents** form reactive carbonium ions that attach alkyl groups to the **N7 of guanine** in DNA → cross-linking of DNA strands, abnormal base pairing, strand breaks → cell death. **Cyclophosphamide** is a prodrug activated by liver CYP enzymes; its metabolite **acrolein** causes haemorrhagic cystitis. Also used as an immunosuppressant. **Cisplatin** forms intrastrand DNA cross-links; used in testicular, ovarian, lung, head and neck cancers.
- **Methotrexate** inhibits **dihydrofolate reductase** → no tetrahydrofolate → no thymidylate and purines → S-phase arrest. Used in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, choriocarcinoma, osteosarcoma; at low doses in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. **Folinic acid (leucovorin)** bypasses the block and rescues normal cells.
- **5-Fluorouracil** is converted to 5-FdUMP, which inhibits **thymidylate synthase**; used in colorectal, breast and skin cancers. **6-Mercaptopurine** inhibits purine synthesis; it is metabolised by **xanthine oxidase**, so with allopurinol its dose must be reduced.
- **Vinca alkaloids** bind tubulin and **prevent microtubule assembly** → metaphase arrest. Vincristine → neuropathy (spares marrow); vinblastine → marrow suppression.
- **Taxanes** do the opposite: they **stabilise microtubules** and prevent their breakdown → mitotic arrest. Paclitaxel → hypersensitivity, neuropathy, neutropenia.
- **Etoposide** inhibits **topoisomerase II**; **topotecan/irinotecan** inhibit **topoisomerase I**.
- **Anthracyclines** (doxorubicin) intercalate DNA, inhibit topoisomerase II and generate free radicals → cumulative **cardiotoxicity** (dexrazoxane protects). Red urine.
- **Bleomycin** forms iron-oxygen complexes that break DNA (G2 phase); little marrow toxicity; pulmonary fibrosis.
- **L-Asparaginase** breaks down asparagine; leukaemic cells cannot make their own asparagine.
- **Tamoxifen** blocks oestrogen receptors in breast (used in receptor-positive breast cancer) but acts as an agonist in the uterus (endometrial cancer risk) and bone.

### Drug resistance in cancer

Mechanisms: reduced uptake, increased efflux by **P-glycoprotein** (multidrug resistance gene MDR1), increased target enzyme (DHFR amplification), increased DNA repair, altered target, failure of apoptosis. Combination therapy and adequate intensity reduce it.

## 4.5 Immunopharmacology: introduction

The immune response has innate and adaptive arms. Adaptive immunity involves **T cells** (cell-mediated; CD4 helper and CD8 cytotoxic) and **B cells** (antibodies). Antigen-presenting cells show antigen to T cells; activated T cells make **interleukin-2 (IL-2)**, which drives T-cell proliferation. Many immunosuppressants act on this pathway.

```text
 Antigen + APC --> T-cell receptor --> calcineurin activated
                                             |
                    cyclosporine/tacrolimus  X  (block calcineurin)
                                             v
                         NFAT --> IL-2 gene transcription --> IL-2
                                             |
                       basiliximab X (blocks IL-2 receptor)
                                             v
                        IL-2 receptor --> mTOR --> T-cell proliferation
                                    sirolimus, everolimus X (block mTOR)
                                             |
      azathioprine, mycophenolate X (block purine synthesis in dividing T cells)
```

## 4.6 Immunosuppressants

**Uses:** prevention and treatment of organ transplant rejection (kidney, liver, heart, bone marrow), graft-versus-host disease, autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia), nephrotic syndrome.

| Class | Examples | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcineurin inhibitors | Cyclosporine, tacrolimus | Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, tacrolimus binds FKBP-12 → complex inhibits calcineurin → no IL-2 transcription |
| mTOR inhibitors | Sirolimus (rapamycin), everolimus | Bind FKBP-12 → inhibit mTOR → block IL-2-driven proliferation |
| Antiproliferative / antimetabolites | Azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, leflunomide | Azathioprine → 6-MP (purine synthesis); mycophenolate inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (guanine synthesis in lymphocytes) |
| Glucocorticoids | Prednisolone, methylprednisolone | Reduce cytokine gene expression (IL-1, IL-2, TNF), lymphocyte redistribution, anti-inflammatory |
| Antibodies | Antithymocyte globulin (polyclonal); basiliximab (anti-IL-2 receptor α); rituximab (anti-CD20); belatacept (blocks co-stimulation) | Deplete or block lymphocytes |
| Anti-cytokine biologicals | Infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept (anti-TNF-α); tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) | Block inflammatory cytokines |

**Cyclosporine:** narrow therapeutic index, blood levels monitored; metabolised by CYP3A4 (levels raised by ketoconazole, erythromycin, diltiazem, grapefruit juice; lowered by rifampicin, phenytoin). Adverse effects: **nephrotoxicity** (main), hypertension, hyperkalaemia, hepatotoxicity, **hirsutism**, **gum hyperplasia**, tremor, diabetes. It does not suppress the bone marrow. **Tacrolimus** is more potent; causes nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and diabetes but less hirsutism and gum hyperplasia.

**Azathioprine:** bone marrow suppression; dose reduced with allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibition); TPMT enzyme deficiency increases toxicity. **Mycophenolate:** GI upset, leucopenia, teratogenic.

**General risks of immunosuppression:** opportunistic infections (CMV, fungi, *Pneumocystis*), reactivation of TB and hepatitis B, and higher risk of lymphoma and skin cancer. Combinations of drugs with different mechanisms (triple therapy, e.g. tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone) allow lower amounts of each.

## 4.7 Immunostimulants

Drugs that enhance immune responses in immunodeficiency, chronic infections and some cancers.

| Example | Use |
| --- | --- |
| BCG (live attenuated *M. bovis*) | Vaccine against TB; intravesical BCG in superficial bladder cancer |
| Levamisole | Originally an anthelmintic; restores T-cell function (older use in colon cancer adjuvant therapy, nephrotic syndrome in children) |
| Interferons: α (hepatitis B and C, hairy cell leukaemia, Kaposi sarcoma), β (multiple sclerosis), γ (chronic granulomatous disease) | Antiviral, antiproliferative, immunomodulatory; cause flu-like symptoms, depression, marrow suppression |
| Interleukin-2 (aldesleukin) | Metastatic renal cell carcinoma and melanoma |
| Colony-stimulating factors: filgrastim (G-CSF), sargramostim (GM-CSF) | Raise neutrophil counts after chemotherapy |
| Thymic peptides (thymosin), inosine pranobex, imiquimod | Immunomodulators; imiquimod stimulates local interferon (genital warts, skin cancers) |
| Immunoglobulins | Passive immunity, immunodeficiency |
| Vaccines | Active immunisation |
| Immune checkpoint inhibitors: pembrolizumab, nivolumab (anti-PD-1), ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) | Release the "brakes" on T cells in cancer; immune-related adverse effects (colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis) |
| Herbal immunomodulators | *Withania somnifera* (ashwagandha), *Tinospora cordifolia* (guduchi), *Echinacea* — traditional use |

## 4.8 Protein drugs, monoclonal antibodies, targeted drugs and biosimilars

### Protein drugs

Proteins made by **recombinant DNA technology** in bacteria, yeast or mammalian cells: insulin, growth hormone, erythropoietin, filgrastim, interferons, tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase), clotting factors, enzymes for enzyme replacement (imiglucerase), and hormones such as FSH.

**Features:** large molecules, destroyed in the gut, so given by injection; may be immunogenic (form antibodies); need cold storage (2–8 °C); **pegylation** (attaching polyethylene glycol) prolongs action (peginterferon, pegfilgrastim).

### Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs)

Identical antibodies from a single clone of cells, originally made by **hybridoma technology** (fusion of an antibody-producing B cell with a myeloma cell). The suffix of the name tells its origin and target:

| Suffix | Source | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| -omab | Mouse | Muromonab-CD3 (older) |
| -ximab | Chimeric (mouse variable + human constant) | Rituximab, infliximab, basiliximab, cetuximab |
| -zumab | Humanised | Trastuzumab, bevacizumab, omalizumab, tocilizumab |
| -umab | Fully human | Adalimumab, denosumab, nivolumab |

**Mechanisms:** neutralise a ligand (bevacizumab binds VEGF; infliximab binds TNF-α), block a receptor (trastuzumab on HER2; cetuximab on EGFR), mark cells for destruction by complement and immune cells (rituximab on CD20 of B cells), or deliver a toxin/drug (**antibody–drug conjugates** such as trastuzumab emtansine).

| mAb | Target | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rituximab | CD20 | Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, CLL, rheumatoid arthritis |
| Trastuzumab | HER2/neu | HER2-positive breast cancer (cardiotoxicity) |
| Bevacizumab | VEGF | Colorectal cancer, age-related macular degeneration (off-label; ranibizumab is the eye-specific form) |
| Cetuximab | EGFR | Colorectal, head and neck cancers |
| Infliximab, adalimumab | TNF-α | Rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, psoriasis (screen for latent TB first) |
| Omalizumab | IgE | Severe allergic asthma |
| Denosumab | RANKL | Osteoporosis |
| Basiliximab | IL-2 receptor | Transplant rejection prophylaxis |

**Adverse effects:** infusion reactions, hypersensitivity, infections (TB reactivation with anti-TNF drugs), formation of anti-drug antibodies, target-specific effects.

### Targeted drugs (drugs aimed at a specific molecular target)

Small molecules that block signals cancer cells depend on — usually **kinase inhibitors** (suffix **-tinib**):

| Drug | Target | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Imatinib | **BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase** (Philadelphia chromosome), c-KIT | Chronic myeloid leukaemia (first "magic bullet" success), GIST |
| Gefitinib, erlotinib | EGFR tyrosine kinase | Non-small cell lung cancer with EGFR mutation |
| Sorafenib, sunitinib | VEGFR and other kinases | Renal cell and liver cancer |
| Bortezomib | Proteasome | Multiple myeloma |

Targeted drugs (small molecules and mAbs) are more selective than cytotoxic drugs, so they cause less marrow suppression, but they have their own effects (skin rash, diarrhoea, hypertension, fluid retention) and resistance develops through target mutation. "Targeting drugs to an antigen" also includes **antibody–drug conjugates** and radio-labelled antibodies, which carry a cytotoxic or radioactive payload to cells bearing the antigen.

### Biosimilars

A **biosimilar** is a biological product that is **highly similar** to an already approved reference biological, with **no clinically meaningful differences** in safety, purity and potency. Because biologicals are made in living cells by complex processes, an exact copy cannot be made (unlike generic small-molecule drugs, which are chemically identical).

| Generic drug | Biosimilar |
| --- | --- |
| Small, simple, chemically defined molecule | Large, complex protein |
| Identical to the reference | Similar, not identical |
| Bioequivalence study is enough | Stepwise comparability: analytical, non-clinical, clinical (PK/PD, immunogenicity, efficacy) |
| Low development cost | Higher cost, but cheaper than the original biological |

In India, biosimilars are approved under the **"Similar Biologics" guidelines** of CDSCO and the Department of Biotechnology. Examples: biosimilar trastuzumab, rituximab, adalimumab, insulin glargine, filgrastim, erythropoietin. India was among the early countries to market biosimilars, which has improved access to costly biological therapy.

## Remember

- UTI: *E. coli* commonest; nitrofurantoin acts only in urine (avoid in renal failure); methenamine needs acidic urine (releases formaldehyde); fosfomycin single oral dose.
- STD: syndromic approach; syphilis → benzathine penicillin; gonorrhoea → ceftriaxone; chlamydia → azithromycin/doxycycline; trichomonas → metronidazole.
- Log-kill: a fixed fraction killed per course; combination and cyclic therapy.
- Alkylating agents → guanine N7; cyclophosphamide → acrolein → haemorrhagic cystitis → mesna.
- Methotrexate → DHFR, rescue with folinic acid; 5-FU → thymidylate synthase; 6-MP with allopurinol needs less.
- Vinca prevents microtubule assembly, taxanes prevent disassembly; etoposide topo II, topotecan topo I.
- Doxorubicin → cardiotoxic; bleomycin → lung fibrosis; cisplatin → kidney, ear, vomiting; vincristine → neuropathy.
- Cyclosporine/tacrolimus → calcineurin → IL-2; sirolimus → mTOR; mycophenolate → IMP dehydrogenase; cyclosporine nephrotoxic, hirsutism, gum hyperplasia.
- Immunostimulants: BCG, levamisole, interferons, IL-2, G-CSF, checkpoint inhibitors.
- mAb suffixes: -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human; rituximab CD20, trastuzumab HER2, bevacizumab VEGF, infliximab TNF.
- Imatinib → BCR-ABL in CML. Biosimilar = highly similar, not identical; India's Similar Biologics guidelines.

# Unit 5: Principles of toxicology and chronopharmacology

The last unit is short in teaching hours but easy to score in. It has two parts: **toxicology** (types of toxicity, the special toxicities tested before a drug is marketed, and the general plan for managing a poisoned patient) and **chronopharmacology** (how the body's daily rhythms change drug action, and how drug timing is planned around them).

> Scope of these notes: the poisoning topics are covered at the level of definitions, the general principles of management as a textbook chapter lists them, and the named antidotes by class. Treatment of an actual poisoning is always decided by the treating doctor and the Poison Information Centre. For the clinical features of each named poisoning, read the chapter in your prescribed textbook.

## 5.1 Basic terms in toxicology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Toxicology | Science that studies the harmful effects of chemicals (drugs, industrial and household chemicals, natural toxins) on living organisms, their detection, mechanisms and management |
| Poison | Any substance that can cause harm or death when it enters the body in sufficient amount ("the dose makes the poison" — Paracelsus) |
| Toxicity | The degree to which a substance can harm an organism |
| Hazard vs risk | Hazard is the capacity to cause harm; risk is the probability that harm occurs under given exposure |
| LD50 (median lethal dose) | Dose that kills 50% of the test animals in a defined period; a measure of acute toxicity (determined statistically in the laboratory; see the BP608P practical) |
| ED50 | Dose that produces the desired effect in 50% of animals |
| Therapeutic index | LD50 ÷ ED50 (or TD50 ÷ ED50 in humans); higher means safer |
| NOAEL | No-observed-adverse-effect level: highest dose in a study with no harmful effect |
| Branches | Clinical, forensic, environmental, occupational, regulatory and analytical toxicology |

**Routes of exposure:** oral, inhalation, skin and eye contact, injection. **Types by cause:** accidental (children, occupational), suicidal, homicidal, iatrogenic (drug-induced), and environmental.

## 5.2 Acute, subacute and chronic toxicity

Toxicity studies are classified by how long animals are exposed. They are required before human trials and marketing (Schedule Y / New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019 in India; OECD test guidelines internationally).

| Type | Definition | Exposure and observation | What it tells |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acute toxicity | Harmful effects after a **single** exposure (or several within 24 h) | Observed for 14 days | LD50 or acute toxic class, signs of toxicity, target organs; guides dose selection for later studies |
| Subacute (repeated-dose 28-day) toxicity | Effects of **repeated daily** exposure for a short period | 14–28 days | Target organs, reversibility, dose for longer studies |
| Subchronic toxicity | Repeated exposure for part of the lifespan | Usually 90 days | NOAEL, cumulative effects |
| Chronic toxicity | Repeated exposure for a **long** part of the lifespan | 6 months (rodents) to 9–12 months (non-rodents) or longer | Long-term organ damage, accumulation, safety margin for long-term human use |

**Parameters examined:** clinical signs and behaviour, body weight, food and water intake, haematology, serum biochemistry (liver and kidney tests), urine analysis, organ weights, and histopathology of organs at the end. Usually done in a rodent (rat) and a non-rodent (dog, rabbit) of both sexes at three dose levels with a control group.

**Acute vs chronic toxicity in humans**

| Feature | Acute | Chronic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exposure | Single or short | Repeated over months or years |
| Onset | Quick | Slow, gradual |
| Effects | Often reversible | Often cumulative, may be irreversible (organ damage, cancer) |
| Example pattern | Accidental single exposure | Occupational exposure to heavy metals |

**Modern approach (3Rs):** reduction, refinement and replacement of animal use. The classical LD50 test needing many animals has been replaced by methods using fewer animals: the **fixed dose procedure** (OECD 420), **acute toxic class method** (OECD 423) and **up-and-down procedure** (OECD 425). In India, animal studies follow **CCSEA** (formerly CPCSEA) guidelines and need approval of the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee.

## 5.3 Genotoxicity, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity and teratogenicity

| Term | Definition | Common tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Genotoxicity** | Any damage to the genetic material (DNA, chromosomes), whether or not it is inherited — strand breaks, adducts, chromosome damage | Comet assay, chromosomal aberration test, micronucleus test, unscheduled DNA synthesis |
| **Mutagenicity** | Ability to cause a **permanent, heritable change** (mutation) in the DNA sequence — point mutations, frameshifts, chromosome changes. All mutagens are genotoxic, not all genotoxic agents cause lasting mutation | **Ames test** (reverse mutation in histidine-dependent *Salmonella typhimurium* strains, with liver S9 fraction for metabolic activation), mouse lymphoma assay, in vivo micronucleus test |
| **Carcinogenicity** | Ability to cause **cancer** (malignant tumours). Genotoxic carcinogens damage DNA directly; non-genotoxic (epigenetic) carcinogens act by hormonal effects, chronic irritation or cell proliferation | Long-term rodent bioassay (usually 2 years in rats and mice), transgenic mouse models; needed for drugs used long term |
| **Teratogenicity** | Ability to cause **structural or functional defects in the embryo or fetus** when given during pregnancy | Reproductive and developmental toxicity studies (fertility, embryo-fetal development in two species, pre- and postnatal development) |

**Carcinogenesis in stages:** initiation (irreversible DNA change) → promotion (clonal growth of initiated cells) → progression (malignancy and spread). Examples of drugs/chemicals linked to cancer: alkylating agents (secondary leukaemia), oestrogens (endometrial cancer), tamoxifen (endometrium), cyclophosphamide (bladder), benzene, aflatoxin, tobacco smoke, asbestos.

**Teratogenesis — key points:**

- The most sensitive period is **organogenesis** (about the 3rd to 8th week after conception). Before that, damage is "all or none"; later, it causes growth and functional defects.
- Classic example: **thalidomide** (1950s–60s) → phocomelia (short, flipper-like limbs). This disaster led to modern drug regulation and compulsory reproductive toxicity testing.
- Other known teratogens: isotretinoin and other retinoids, warfarin (fetal warfarin syndrome), valproate (neural tube defects), phenytoin (fetal hydantoin syndrome), ACE inhibitors (fetal kidney damage in later pregnancy), tetracyclines (teeth and bones), methotrexate, lithium (Ebstein's anomaly), diethylstilboestrol (vaginal cancer in daughters), alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome).
- Drugs in pregnancy are grouped by risk categories in many references; the principle is to use a drug only when clearly needed, choose the one with the longest safety record, and avoid the first trimester where possible.

## 5.4 General principles of treatment of poisoning

Management of a poisoned patient is a medical emergency handled by doctors and Poison Information Centres. For the exam, learn the headings in order, as textbook chapters list them:

1. **Resuscitation and stabilisation** — airway, breathing and circulation first.
2. **Diagnosis** — history, examination and laboratory analysis to identify the substance.
3. **Decontamination** — measures that limit further exposure.
4. **Enhanced elimination** — measures that increase removal of an absorbed substance, used only for selected cases.
5. **Specific antidote** — where one exists.
6. **Supportive care and monitoring** — the backbone of treatment, because most poisons have no antidote.
7. **Prevention and follow-up** — counselling, safe storage, reporting to a Poison Information Centre.

**Antidote** means a substance that counteracts the effect of a poison. Antidotes are grouped by how they work: receptor antagonists, enzyme reactivators, chelating agents (bind metals into a complex the body can excrete), and agents that restore a protective body substance.

## 5.5 Named antidotes for the syllabus poisonings

| Poisoning named in syllabus | Antidote or approach (by name and class) |
| --- | --- |
| Barbiturates | No specific antidote; supportive care |
| Morphine (opioids) | Naloxone — opioid receptor antagonist |
| Organophosphorus compounds | Atropine — muscarinic antagonist; pralidoxime — oxime cholinesterase reactivator |
| Lead | Chelating agents: calcium disodium edetate, dimercaprol (BAL), succimer (DMSA), penicillamine |
| Mercury | Chelating agents: dimercaprol, succimer, unithiol (DMPS) |
| Arsenic | Chelating agents: dimercaprol, succimer, unithiol |

Other antidote pairs often asked as MCQs: N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol), flumazenil (benzodiazepines), protamine (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin), desferrioxamine (iron), fomepizole (methanol), digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin).

## 5.6 Chronopharmacology: definitions

**Chronopharmacology** is the study of how the effects and kinetics of drugs vary with biological time (the time of day, month or year), and of how drugs themselves change biological rhythms.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Biological rhythm | A regular, self-sustained, repeating change in a body function |
| Cycle | One complete repetition of a rhythm |
| Period | Time taken for one cycle |
| Amplitude | Half the difference between the highest and lowest value |
| Acrophase | Time at which the rhythm peaks |
| MESOR | Rhythm-adjusted mean value |
| Circadian rhythm | Period of about 24 h (Latin *circa diem*): sleep–wake, body temperature, cortisol, blood pressure |
| Ultradian rhythm | Period shorter than 24 h: heartbeat, breathing, pulsatile hormone release |
| Infradian rhythm | Period longer than 24 h: menstrual cycle (circamensual), seasonal or yearly (circannual) |
| Zeitgeber | External time cue that sets the clock; light–dark cycle is the main one |

**Branches:**

- **Chronopharmacokinetics** — rhythmic changes in absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (gastric emptying, liver blood flow, kidney function vary through the day).
- **Chronopharmacodynamics (chronesthesy)** — rhythmic changes in the sensitivity of target tissues and receptors.
- **Chronotoxicology** — variation of adverse effects with the time of drug use.
- **Chronotherapy** — timing drug use to match the body's rhythms, for better effect and fewer adverse effects.

## 5.7 Biological clock and its significance

```text
 Light --> retina --> retinohypothalamic tract
                            |
                            v
          Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), hypothalamus  = master clock
                            |
          +-----------------+------------------+
          v                 v                  v
     Pineal gland      Cortisol rhythm    Peripheral clocks
     melatonin (night) (peak early morning) liver, heart, gut, kidney
```

- The **master clock** is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** of the hypothalamus. It is reset daily by light and keeps peripheral clocks in organs in step.
- At the molecular level, **clock genes** (CLOCK, BMAL1, Period, Cryptochrome) form feedback loops of transcription and translation lasting about 24 h.
- The **pineal gland** releases **melatonin** in darkness; melatonin and its agonists (ramelteon, agomelatine) are used for sleep and jet-lag problems.
- Disturbance of the clock (shift work, jet lag) is linked with sleep disorders, metabolic and mood problems.

**Significance leading to chronotherapy — examples**

| Condition / rhythm | Chronotherapy point |
| --- | --- |
| Asthma worsens at night and early morning (low cortisol and adrenaline, high vagal tone) | Evening doses of inhaled steroids or long-acting bronchodilators; theophylline timed for night cover |
| Blood pressure surges in the early morning; heart attacks and strokes more common then | Timing of antihypertensives to cover the morning rise |
| Cholesterol synthesis is highest at night | Short-acting statins (simvastatin) given in the evening |
| Gastric acid secretion peaks at night | Bedtime H2-blocker for ulcer healing |
| Cortisol peaks in the early morning | Corticosteroids given in the morning reduce suppression of the adrenal axis |
| Rheumatoid arthritis stiffness is worst in the morning | Delayed-release preparations taken at bedtime |
| Cancer cells and normal cells differ in rhythm | Timed anticancer drug use to reduce toxicity |

**Chronotherapeutic drug delivery systems** (pulsatile or delayed-release dosage forms) release drug after a lag time so that the peak level comes when the disease is most active, for example a bedtime dose releasing in the early morning.

## Remember

- Acute = single exposure, observed 14 days; subacute = repeated 28 days; subchronic = 90 days; chronic = 6 months or more.
- Genotoxic = any DNA damage; mutagenic = heritable change (Ames test); carcinogenic = cancer (2-year rodent study); teratogenic = birth defects (thalidomide → phocomelia; organogenesis weeks 3–8).
- 3Rs and fewer-animal acute methods (OECD 420, 423, 425); CCSEA approval.
- Poisoning management headings: stabilise → diagnose → decontaminate → enhance elimination → antidote → support → prevent.
- Antidotes: naloxone (opioids), atropine + pralidoxime (organophosphates), chelators for lead, mercury, arsenic; barbiturates have no specific antidote.
- Circadian ≈ 24 h, ultradian < 24 h, infradian > 24 h; SCN is the master clock; melatonin at night.
- Chronotherapy: evening statin, morning steroid, night cover in asthma, bedtime H2-blocker.
